lead: Today the Panchangam remembers Ezekiel the Prophet, the watchman among the exiles, who warned his people and also promised them a new heart and a new spirit. Both readings speak to a people in a hard time. Paul thanks the Father who has rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of his Son. In the Gospel Jesus warns the disciples of wars, false teachers, hatred and cold love, and promises: “the one who endures to the end will be saved.” The key words are rescued, watch and endure.

r.h: Rescued from darkness into the kingdom
set: After the greeting, Paul tells the Colossians that he thanks God for their faith and love (1:3–8) and prays that they may be filled with the knowledge of God's will (1:9–11). Our verses continue that prayer in the form of thanksgiving, and they lead straight into the great hymn to Christ, the image of the invisible God (1:15–20).

Paul's words are rich with the memory of Israel. The “inheritance” recalls the land given to Israel as its share, and the “rescue” is the vocabulary of the Exodus. What God did for Israel in bringing it out of Egypt, he has now done in Christ for those who believe, whether Jew or Gentile.
str: v. 12: thanksgiving to the Father, who has made us fit to share the inheritance of the saints in light.
v. 13: he rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son.
v. 14: in the Son we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
kw: The word for a portion assigned by lot, the share of the land that each tribe received. Here the share is “in the light”, a place in God's own life, which is given and not earned.
The word was used for moving a whole people from one land to another. We have been moved out of one kingdom into another, as the people of Israel passed from Egypt to the land of promise.
Literally a release by the payment of a ransom. In the Old Testament it recalls the release of slaves and Israel's rescue from Egypt. Paul identifies it with the forgiveness of sins.
vv: giving thanks to the Father, who has enabled you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light.
Paul begins with thanks. Our place in the light is something we have been enabled to receive. It is the Father's gift, and the right response to a gift is gratitude.
He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son,
Paul uses the past tense: it has happened. “His beloved Son” is literally “the Son of his love”, so the kingdom is the kingdom of the one whom the Father loves, and we are brought into that love.
in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.
Some later manuscripts add “through his blood” here, from Ephesians 1:7; it is not in the oldest ones. The truth of the added words is clear from other texts, such as Colossians 1:20.
ch: The Church sees in these verses the meaning of Baptism, in which we are delivered from sin and from the power of the evil one and brought into the family of God. The rite of Baptism includes exorcisms that express this liberation (CCC 1237), and the Catechism teaches that by Baptism all sins are forgiven (CCC 1263). The Syriac Fathers loved to speak of the font as a womb from which the baptized are born again, clothed in a robe of glory (Mar Aphrem, in substance). Giving thanks, as Paul does, is also the meaning of the Eucharist, which in Greek means “thanksgiving”, the Church's prayer of gratitude for being rescued.

r.h: The one who endures to the end
set: Jesus has just left the Temple and told his disciples that not one stone will be left on another (24:1–2). On the Mount of Olives, facing the Temple, they ask him privately: when will this be, and what will be the sign of his coming and of the end of the age? This is the beginning of the long discourse of Matthew 24–25, often called the Olivet Discourse. Many interpreters see in it both the coming destruction of the Temple and the end of the age, spoken of together, as the prophets often did.

Our verses are the first part. Jesus does not give dates or maps. He gives the disciples a way to live in the time between his departure and his return: do not be led astray, do not be alarmed, stay faithful, and preach the Gospel to all nations.
str: vv. 3–4: the disciples' question and the first warning: do not be led astray.
vv. 5–8: false messiahs, wars and rumours, famines and earthquakes: only the beginning of the birth pangs.
vv. 9–12: persecution, falling away, betrayal, false prophets, and the cooling of love.
vv. 13–14: endurance leads to salvation; the Gospel is preached to all the nations, and then the end.
kw: The pains of a woman in labour. In the Old Testament the pains of childbirth are an image for the trials that come before God acts (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–9). Pains that lead to a birth are not meaningless.

Not passive waiting but staying under a load and holding on. It is the great virtue of the disciple in a hard time, and the same word family appears in Paul's prayer just before our verses, that the Colossians may be prepared to endure everything with patience (Colossians 1:11).

The Gospel will be proclaimed “as a testimony to all the nations”. The word is the root of martyr: the witness of disciples, sometimes at the price of their lives, is how the good news reaches the world.
vv: Jesus answered them, “Beware that no one leads you astray.
The first danger Jesus names is not persecution but deception. The disciples need clear eyes more than fearful hearts.
all this is but the beginning of the birth pangs.
Wars and disasters are not the end. They show a world still in labour. Jesus tells his disciples not to read every shock as the final sign, and not to panic.
And because of the increase of lawlessness, the love of many will grow cold.
The saddest line of the passage. The danger within the community is not only the enemy outside but the loss of love inside. The remedy is to keep love warm.
But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
Salvation is promised to those who hold on in faith, and it is God's grace that makes holding on possible. The disciple does not endure by his own strength alone.
And this good news of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the world, as a testimony to all the nations; and then the end will come.

The Church's mission is not a side matter. The Gospel goes out to all peoples, and this is part of how history moves to its end. The same promise stands at the end of the Gospel: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (28:19).
ch: The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension, Christ's coming in glory is imminent, yet no one knows the day or the hour, and the times belong to the Father (CCC 673). Before his coming the Church will pass through a final trial that will shake the faith of many believers (CCC 675). The Church reads Jesus' words not as a timetable, but as a call to watchfulness, mission and faithfulness. Hope, the Catechism says, means that each of us should hope, with the grace of God, to persevere to the end (CCC 1821). Today many Christians in many lands suffer for their faith, and others suffer for other reasons; we pray for all who suffer, and for those who wrong them, that their hearts may be changed.

qa: Does this passage tell us when the world will end?

No. Jesus warns against exactly that kind of calculation. A few verses later he says that about “that day and hour” no one knows, “neither the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (24:36). The Church has always rejected attempts to fix dates. What the passage gives is a way of life: watch, do not be afraid, keep love warm, hold on, and proclaim the Gospel.
study: Paul says the Father has “rescued us from the power of darkness”. What has God rescued me from, and have I given thanks for it?
Jesus says the love of many will grow cold. What helps me to keep my love warm: in my family, in my parish, towards people I find difficult?
